newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Money pours into Brazil stocks as LatAm star rises.
newsitem.headline: Money pours into Brazil stocks as LatAm star rises.

text.p: Capital flows to Brazil's stock markets are surging as foreign investors adjust portfolios and cut positions in Asia and the United States in favor of brighter horizons in Latin America, banking and market specialists said.
"There is a consensus that Brazil is a good risk this year," said Luiz Eduardo Assis, a senior investment officer at Citibank's local unit.
Seasonally high capital flows, as investors readjust stock portfolios for the year, have helped boost local stock prices 8.7 percent so far in 1997, market sources said.

But fund managers and equities specialists told Reuters that prices and daily volumes are getting an added boost from investors seeking higher returns than those expected in Asia and the United States.

U.S. markets in 1997 are not likely to repeat last year's strong run-up while Asian stocks are expected to be hurt by slowing economic growth, rising public deficits and political turbulence, they said.
"So capital should flow to areas of higher growth and political stability. Amazingly, that's Latin America," said Saulo Holzman, an asset manager with BBA Capital in Sao Paulo.
He said investors are heartened by political continuity in Argentina and Peru and economic progress in Mexico and Brazil.
Daily turnover on the Sao Paulo bourse has soared to more than $700 million this week from average volumes of half that figure last year, although the strong trade is expected to wane after January.
Market experts said the strong foreign capital flows actually began late in 1996, when investors started assessing the prospects of Brazilian stocks for this year and began taking positions.

Brazil's Securities Commission (CVM) said net capital inflows to Brazilian bourses under Annex Four rules totalled $560.7 million in December, more than the $528.2 million posted in all of 1995. Total net foreign capital inflows in 1996 reached $3.593 billion, it said.

Julius Buchenrode, a director of Unibanco brokerage and investment bank, said the recent surge in stock trade stems mostly from institutional investors reshuffling stock portfolios, something they do every January.
As a result, current hefty stock volume is likely to taper off as the year wears on, he said.

He added that investors also may be entering the bolsa now to avoid the new 0.2 percent CPMF financial transactions tax due to take effect Jan 23 though others said long-term foreign investors are not really concerned about the levy.

Market experts said dollar capital inflows are not the only factor affecting the bolsas' rise. "Foreign investors are very interested in Brazil, particularly if the government continues sending signals that it remains committed to stabilization and reform," Buchenrode said.
Investors are especially interested in Brazil's plans to privatize its telecommunications, energy and mining sectors, all expected to move ahead this year, Holzman said.
Assis said investors also are upbeat about Brazil's economic fundamentals, such as inflation, public deficit and currency depreciation. "The only concern is the trade deficit," he said.
Moreover, many Brazilian stocks, including blue chips like Telebras, are drastically undervalued, he said.

"At the end of 1996, the Bovespa index in dollar terms was below where it was when President Fernando Henrique Cardoso took office two years ago," Assis said. "Things have changed a lot since then, so there is a lot of space to rise."
Fund managers and analysts forecast the Sao Paulo bourse will rise between 25 and 40 percent in dollar terms this year.
((--Sao Paulo newsroom 5511 248 5413))
